_note: PLACEHOLDER DIALOGUE FOR DIRECTOR REVIEW. Character names are placeholders. No line is a genuine quotation; lines with a 'paraphrase' field paraphrase the cited BG chapter. Provenance tags per beat: documented | plausible | fictional. Beats with approval:true need director sign-off before production.

centurion.name: Titus Arrius
centurion.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Fictional. Newly promoted in 58 BCE, about 28. Dry, quick, proud, wants Caesar's notice. Speaks less as the campaign goes on; by Act III he speaks in Caesar's cadence. Ends alive, at Uxellodunum, looking at his hands.

caesar.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
caesar.notes: Historical. Warm, funny, exact, brave, never raises his voice to be obeyed. Explains atrocity with clarity and composure. No personality switch: the man in ch12 is the man in ch1. All lines are placeholder invention unless tagged as a paraphrase of BG.

sextus.name: Sextus Naevius
sextus.role: Optio of the centurion's century; his closest friend
sextus.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Teases the centurion relentlessly in Act I. Never a moralist. Comes to fear his friend's composure, not his rage. The tell is that he stops calling him Titus.

fufius.name: Gnaeus Fufius
fufius.role: Tesserarius; later lent to the quaestor as tally clerk
fufius.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Good with numbers, fussy, kind to mules. Counting captives at the Aduatuci upsets him; by Alesia he runs the distribution, and at Uxellodunum he keeps the tally. Becomes cruel through routine, not appetite.

bassus.name: Bassus
bassus.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Runs a book on everything. Never stops being cheerful, and that becomes one of the most disturbing things in the game.

opimius.name: Opimius
opimius.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Sings on the march in Act I. Gavius's tent-mate. Speaks less and less after Britain; in Act IV he says almost nothing and does what he is told.

gavius.name: Publius Gavius
gavius.role: Veteran legionary; writes letters for men who cannot
gavius.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. In his forties. The older comrade. Mentors the recruit Tiro. Dies in the surf off Britain, 55 BCE. His letter formula ('The food is bad. The centurion is fair.') outlives him.

tiro.name: Decimus, called Tiro
tiro.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Ploughboy from the Po valley. Worships the centurion as the centurion worships Caesar. Hears the argument at Avaricum. Dies at Gergovia carrying the centurion's message.

ritumara.name: Ritumara
ritumara.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Fictional Aeduan noblewoman attached to the grain contracts. Has a brother in Aeduan politics and a son, Tascos. Ally in 58, leaves when the Aedui break with Rome in 52, captured with the relief army and set aside at Alesia as one of the useful Aedui, translates again in 51 because her son is a hostage.

labienus.name: Titus Labienus
labienus.notes: Historical. Dry, professional, the soldier's officer. Never sentimental. Presence in a given scene is tagged.

aquilifer.name: Aquilifer of the Tenth
aquilifer.notes: Historical but unnamed (BG 4.25). One paraphrased line. Do not give him a name.

vercingetorix.name: Vercingetorix
vercingetorix.notes: Historical. Seen, not heard: he surrenders at Alesia in silence. No lines on purpose.

tribune.name: Aulus (tribune)
tribune.role: Young military tribune of the Tenth
tribune.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. One of the young men from the city who panicked at Vesontio (BG 1.39). Delivers the Tenth's thanks the next morning (BG 1.41). Sends the centurion as a runner at the Sabis.

recruit.name: Marcus (recruit)
recruit.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Stands where Tiro stood. Receives the argument in Act IV.

legionary.name: Legionary
legionary.role: Generic soldier of another century or legion

mercator.name: Trader
mercator.role: Roman slave dealer following the army
mercator.notes: PLACEHOLDER NAME, not canonical. Polite, brisk, honest by his own lights. BG 2.33 says the buyers reported the count.

chapters.title: The Tenth
chapters.summary: Panic in the camp; laughter in the Tenth. Caesar singles out the centurion for a small kindness, then tells the army he would march with the Tenth alone.

flow.location: Tenth Legion lines, camp at Vesontio, dusk

shot.note: the century around its fire; other legions' tents beyond, some lamps lit inside

line.text: Eight feet tall. I have it from a Sequani wine-seller. Eight feet, and they eat their horses.
Everybody eats horses, if the siege is long enough.
Raw, Opimius. Raw, and still saddled.
Are we writing to your mother or not?
line.dir: patient, stylus poised over a tablet

line.text: Dear mother. The Germans are eight feet tall. Send money.
I'll put seven. She has a weak heart.
What do you put in yours?
Same as always. The food is bad. The centurion is fair.
Fair? He's a tyrant. A small, vindictive, recently promoted tyrant.
line.dir: loud; he knows exactly who is behind him

line.text: Recently promoted, Sextus, which means I still remember where you hide the wine.
Centurion. You're not, ah, sealing anything?
Nothing to leave, tribune. I spent it.
Centurion. Runner from the praetorium. The general wants you.
Wash your face. He'll think we keep you in a ditch.

flow.provenance: Documented: the panic, the tribunes from the city, wills sealed throughout the camp (BG 1.39). Fictional: the century and every line.

lines.text: Stand straight in front of him. He notices everything.
He asked after my knee once, at Geneva. Two years later. My knee.
Book's open, centurion. Height of the first German we see. Three to one on eight feet.
Tonight's word is Venus. Bassus bet on Mars. Third time this week.

flow.provenance: Free walk through the Tenth's lines; banter is fictional.

flow.location: Praetorium fire, camp at Vesontio, night

shot.note: Praetorium fire at dusk; Caesar on the folding stool, table and jug at his elbow

line.text: Arrius. Come into the light. I want to see if you're as tall as the Germans.
line.dir: warm, amused; does not get up

line.text: General.
Second night of the march. A man of yours went down on the road.
You took his shield and his pack, and you didn't break step. I was on the bank. You didn't see me.
He'd turned his ankle, sir. It seemed simpler.
It always seems simpler, to the men who can do it.
I'm told the Tenth is running a book on the height of the Germans.
Bassus, sir. I can have him flogged.
Don't you dare. What are the odds on six feet?
Five to one.
Put me down for a denarius. Six feet, and a bad temper.

shot.note: Caesar pours wine into a plain cup and holds it out

line.text: Drink. It's terrible. Labienus buys it.

shot.note: tighter; Caesar serious

line.text: Half my tribunes are writing their wills. They came out from Rome for the view.
My uncle Marius beat these Germans' grandfathers with men like you. Not with men like them.
Tomorrow I'll say something to the centurions. When I say it, don't look surprised.
What will you say, sir?

shot.note: tighter; Caesar serious

line.text: The truth. Slightly early.
Go on. And Arrius. I'm glad you're with me.

shot.note: same frame as shot 1

flow.provenance: Fictional invention. Context documented: the forced march to Vesontio (BG 1.38), the panic among tribunes from the city (BG 1.39). Caesar was the nephew by marriage of Marius, who beat the Cimbri and Teutones (cited by Caesar, BG 1.40). TEMPLATE SCENE: ch12_s03 mirrors it shot for shot.

lines.text: Wooden swords. Try not to cry, centurion.
Ow. Promotion's made you vicious.
Breathe, Titus. You fight like the Germans are watching.
Yield! I yield, you lunatic!
Pay up, Opimius.

flow.provenance: Dawn drill with practice weapons. Tutorial: attack, block, parry, dodge. Mirrored by ch11_g02.

flow.objective: Report to the council of centurions

lines.text: My ribs want a word with the legate. Bassus made forty sesterces on you. I did the falling down. I want half.
You can have a quarter. You fell down badly.
New book, centurion. Does the army march tonight? The Seventh say no. I'm giving them four to one.
The general wants a denarius on six feet. On your German book.
The general? On my book? Five to one. If he wins I'm ruined, and if he loses I'm flogged.
Third will this morning. Men from the Seventh. I charge a copper and I don't read them back.
Nobody in the Tenth, before you ask. Bassus tried to sell them odds on their own funerals.
Two tribunes asked me for passes to Rome this morning, centurion. Family business, both of them. Same family, I think.
Centurion. If anyone asks, I was never going to send that letter.
What letter, tribune?
Exactly. Thank you.

flow.provenance: Documented: tribunes from the city asked leave to withdraw on various pretexts; wills were sealed throughout the camp; some said the army would not obey the order to march (BG 1.39). Fictional: every exchange, and Bassus's book.

flow.location: Council of centurions before the praetorium, morning

shot.note: dozens of centurions in a half-circle; Caesar standing, no platform

line.text: Since when does a centurion decide where his army marches, or why?
These are the men my uncle Marius beat. The men the Helvetii have beaten for years. And we have just beaten the Helvetii.
I'm told the men will refuse when I give the order to march. That doesn't disturb me in the slightest.
So I'll do now what I meant to do later. We break camp tonight, in the fourth watch.
If no one else follows, I'll go with the Tenth alone. It shall be my praetorian cohort.

shot.note: he does not look surprised

line.text: General. The Tenth thanks you for your good opinion. The Tenth is ready.
You knew.
I was told not to look surprised.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar's speech to the centurions and the Tenth's thanks through its tribunes (BG 1.40-41). Lines are condensed paraphrase. Fictional: the centurion's foreknowledge and the tribune's identity.

flow.objective: Escort the foragers to the forest edge

lines.text: You're the Tenth? Caesar's favourites. My brother says you'll be first in and first dead.
Your Latin's good.
Better than your Gaulish. Your men have been calling every woman in the market mother all week.
My son wants to see an eagle. Keep him away from that Bassus. He'd lose it at dice.

flow.provenance: Grain was to come from Gallic allies (BG 1.40, 1.16). Ritumara and the foraging party are fictional. Scenic walk: open fields into the forest edge.

lines.text: In the trees! Germans!
Gods. Gods.
Titus! Shield up!
Stay down! Stay down!
Look at the size of him. Six feet, if that. Bassus owes Caesar a denarius.

flow.provenance: Invented plausible 58 BCE vignette (see 02_GAMEPLAY_SPEC encounter recipe); no specific skirmish is documented. Act I finisher: desperate.

lines.text: Careful with that. It's Aeduan grain until your general pays for it.
He'll pay. He always pays.
He always promises. The Aedui have been listening to Roman promises since before you were born.
Titus. Look at the trees. Don't turn round. Just look.

flow.provenance: Documented: the army depended on grain promised by the Aedui and other allies, and its slow arrival was a grievance (BG 1.16, 1.40). Fictional: the foraging party and Ritumara's view.

lines.text: They came back for the grain! Keep them off the carts!
Two on the left! Titus, two!
Roman! Behind the cart! Behind!
Down! Stay down! Please!
That's all of them. That's all. You can stop now, Titus.

flow.provenance: Invented plausible 58 BCE vignette; no specific skirmish is documented. Second, larger wave of the same raid: the first time the player fights more than two at once. Act I finisher: desperate.

flow.location: The forest edge, afternoon

shot.note: the carts loaded at the forest edge; two raiders lie in the grass, covered by their own cloaks
the centurion's hands on his knees; they will not stop shaking

line.text: Your hands are going.
They do that.
First one who didn't fall down when you hit him?
First one who looked at me while he did it.
Harudes, I think. Twenty-four thousand of them crossed the Rhine to Ariovistus. My brother counted.
line.dir: looking at the dead man, not at them

line.text: You were shaking. Good. My brother says Romans don't.
Tell your brother I'll practise.

shot.note: the carts move off toward the camp; the light going gold

flow.provenance: Fictional scene. Documented context: Ariovistus had brought 24,000 Harudes across the Rhine (BG 1.31). Act I: the centurion still reacts to killing (North Star 5). 'I'll practise' is the first, joking statement of what he becomes.

flow.location: The road out of Vesontio, fourth watch, before dawn

shot.note: torchlit column; Caesar on horseback riding against the flow

line.text: Arrius! Well? How tall?
Six feet, sir. And a bad temper.
Then Bassus owes me a denarius. Tell him I'll collect it in Rome.
Tenth! You're my cohort now. Try to look like it!
A denarius. He'll remember it, too. He remembers everything.

flow.provenance: Documented: the army marched in the fourth watch as Caesar had said (BG 1.41). Fictional: the exchange.

chapters.title: Knights
chapters.place: The plain of the parley, Upper Alsace (location approximate)
chapters.summary: The Tenth rides to a parley on borrowed horses, takes German stones without replying, and breaks Ariovistus. Caesar's joy at recovering a friend.

flow.location: Horse lines of the Gallic cavalry, morning

title.sub: Before the parley with Ariovistus, 58 BCE

shot.note: legionaries being lifted onto Gallic horses; Gallic riders watching, unimpressed

line.text: That horse is my cousin's. If you break its legs, he'll break yours.
Last time I sat on a horse I was courting Vibia. It was her father's mule. I told her it was a horse.
Caesar's done better than he promised, lads. He said he'd make us his bodyguard. Now he's made us knights!
Sit up, Bassus. Knights don't hold on with their teeth.
Should we expect trouble, sir?
From Ariovistus, always. From you, never. That's why you're on the horses.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar mounted men of the Tenth on the Gallic cavalry's horses, and a soldier of the Tenth made the joke about being made knights (BG 1.42). Fictional: attributing the joke to Bassus, all other lines.

lines.text: Breakfast.
That's my wine.
It was. Drink up. If Ariovistus kills us I'm not leaving it to him.
He likes the marching song. He's the first one in the century who does.
If he throws me, centurion, sing it at my funeral. Slowly. Bassus can't keep time.
Every horse in the Gallic cavalry, centurion, and every one of them has bitten me. I've started counting the bites.
How many?
Eleven. Twelve, if you count Bassus.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar took the horses of the Gallic cavalry and mounted the Tenth on them for the parley (BG 1.42). Fictional: every exchange.

flow.objective: Ride to the station two hundred paces from the mound

lines.text: Ten men each at the mound, all mounted. His terms. Watch his cavalry, not him.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Tenth stationed 200 paces from the mound (BG 1.43). Labienus's presence is plausible, not attested.

flow.location: The plain before the mound

shot.note: two small groups of riders on the mound, far off; gestures, no audible words

line.text: He's reminding Ariovistus who made him a king. Ariovistus is reminding him who has the army.
Riders, left. They're throwing stones.
No one returns a weapon. No one.
I won't have it said I lured them to a parley and cut them down. Let them be the ones who broke it.
Shields! Hold, Tenth. Hold and take it.

flow.provenance: Documented: the conference on horseback and the German cavalry's attack with stones and weapons; Caesar forbade any reply so it could not be said he had trapped them (BG 1.43, 1.46). Lines are condensed paraphrase.

flow.objective: Hold under the stones. Do not strike.

lines.text: Knights don't get to hit back, apparently.
Shield up, Opimius! Up!
Titus, cover! Don't strike, cover!
They've gone. Good. Now the whole army knows who broke it.

rules.note: Block, parry and dodge only; enemies withdraw when the timer ends.

flow.provenance: Mechanic expresses Caesar's documented order not to return a weapon.

flow.location: The plain before the German camp, five days later

shot.note: the legions drawn up in three lines on the plain; the German camp beyond, smoke, nobody coming out

line.text: Five days stood in line in full kit. He won't come out. I've worn a groove in Gaul.
He's marched his camp past ours. He means to cut us off from the Aeduan grain.
Then we'll build a second camp past his. Six hundred paces. Two lines under arms. The third digs.
Arrius. The Tenth is the third line today. I'm told your men dig the way they fight.
Better, sir. The ditch doesn't hit back.
Today it might.

flow.provenance: Documented: five days of Caesar offering battle while Ariovistus kept to camp and moved past Caesar to cut off his supplies; the second camp 600 paces beyond, two lines under arms and the third fortifying (BG 1.48-49). The Tenth as the third line is plausible, not attested. Fictional: the dialogue.

lines.text: Knights last week. Ditch-diggers this week. By next week he'll have us pulling the carts.
Germans on the skyline. Keep digging. The first two lines watch them. You watch your spade.
Here they come. Light troops, thousands of them. Spades down when I say, not before.
Rampart's up. Spades down! Shields!

flow.provenance: Documented: Ariovistus sent about 16,000 light troops and all his cavalry to frighten the men and hinder the work; two lines drove them off while the third completed it (BG 1.49). Same input rhythm as every later work beat.

flow.objective: Hold the lesser camp until sunset

lines.text: Their foot run beside the horses! Hanging off the manes! Watch the runners!
Keep the ditch between you and them! That's what it's for!
Titus! Back to the rampart! Back!
Did you see that? Gavius, write that down! Put it in the letter!
Sunset. They're going back to their wagons. Good work, Tenth.

flow.provenance: Documented: Ariovistus attacked the lesser camp and the fight went on until sunset (BG 1.50); the German horse fought with picked foot-soldiers who ran beside them holding the manes (BG 1.48). New behaviour: skirmisher pairs arriving fast and on a timer, not when the field clears.

flow.location: The lesser camp, night

shot.note: night inside the half-built rampart; a German prisoner sits bound just out of frame, lit by the fire

line.text: Ask him why Ariovistus won't fight. Politely. He's had a long day.
Their matrons cast lots. The lots say the Germans cannot win if they fight before the new moon.
Then we must oblige the gods and fight before it.
Tomorrow, then.
Tomorrow. Arrius, tell your men the moon is on our side. They'll like that.
And if the lots are right?
Then I'll have been beaten by a bag of sticks, and the Senate will finally have something to laugh about.

flow.provenance: Documented: prisoners told Caesar the German matrons had declared by lots and divination that the Germans could not win if they fought before the new moon; the next day Caesar drew up and advanced on their camp (BG 1.50-51). Fictional: Ritumara as interpreter, every line except the paraphrase.

flow.location: Battle line facing the Germans

shot.note: German line; beyond it a ring of wagons with women standing on them

line.text: Look behind their line. Wagons. They've brought their women to watch.
To watch, or to make sure nobody runs.
Tenth! Right wing. I'll be with you.

flow.provenance: Documented: German wagons with women behind the line, begging their men not to let them be enslaved; Caesar led the right wing himself (BG 1.51-52). The Tenth's exact position is not stated: plausible.

lines.text: No room for javelins! Get in close! Pull their shields down!
That's it! That's it!
Breathe. Breathe.
Did you see that? Did Caesar see that?
They're running! To the river, they're running!

flow.provenance: Documented: the lines closed too fast for javelins; legionaries leapt onto the shield wall and tore shields away; the Germans fled to the Rhine (BG 1.52-53).

flow.location: The battle line, the German right pressing

shot.note: the German line in front broken; beyond it, to the left, their right wing re-forming shields into a wall and pushing

line.text: Not all of them. Look left. Their right is still coming. They've locked shields.
Centurion! Young Crassus is sending the third line! Hold here till they reach you!
Tenth! Face left! Nobody steps back!

flow.provenance: Documented: the Germans re-formed in a phalanx; their right pressed the Roman line hard until P. Crassus, commanding the cavalry, sent the third line to relieve it (BG 1.52). Plausible: the Tenth holding its flank while the relief came; the Tenth's role here is not stated.

flow.objective: Hold the flank until the third line comes

lines.text: Pull their shields down! Get on top of them!
He's up on their shields! The centurion's on their shields!
Titus! Behind me! Breathe!
Down! Stay down!
The third line! They're through! Now they're running. Now they're really running!

flow.provenance: Documented: legionaries leapt onto the German shield wall and tore the shields away; the relief by the third line turned the battle and the Germans fled to the Rhine (BG 1.52-53). Act I ceiling: three timed waves of two from one flank, lighter than the Sabis hold (ch03_g03).

flow.location: Among the abandoned wagons, evening

shot.note: empty wagons, a child's blanket on a wheel

line.text: Their women begged them not to let them become your slaves. That's what they were shouting.
Then their men should have won.
That's what my brother would say. He'd say it cheerfully.
They had Procillus in three chains. They cast lots three times whether to burn him, he says, and three times the lots said wait.
That's worth as much to me as the battle. Don't tell the Senate.
He looks after his own.
Yes. His own.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar recovered his interpreter C. Valerius Procillus in triple chains, who said lots were cast three times over burning him; Caesar says this gave him no less pleasure than the victory (BG 1.53). Fictional: the observers and their exchange.

chapters.title: The Sabis
chapters.place: River Sabis, land of the Nervii (often identified with the Sambre; uncertain)
chapters.summary: Ambushed while digging camp. Sent as a runner, the centurion reaches Caesar in the front rank of a collapsing wing. Caesar saves his life. The Tenth arrives.

lines.text: They say the Nervii drink no wine. Won't let a merchant over the border. Imagine living like that.
I'm imagining it. It's horrible. No wonder they're angry.
Our horse are over the river. Skirmishing in the trees. Their riders keep running back into the wood.
Let them run. Dig.

flow.provenance: Documented: the six leading legions measured out and began to fortify the camp while the cavalry skirmished across the river with Nervian horse who kept retreating into the woods (BG 2.19); the Nervii admitted no wine or merchants (BG 2.15). Cold open before the title: the same work rhythm the whole campaign repeats.

flow.location: Hillside above the river Sabis, the camp half dug

shot.note: legionaries digging the camp ditch, helmets off, shields in their covers; river and dense woods below

line.text: Twenty miles, and now we dig a city. Every night he wants a city.
Dig, Bassus. The Nervii don't care about your feet.
A city every night, a road every morning, and Bassus crying every evening.
Helmets off, shields in their covers, Opimius singing. If the Nervii come now they'll die laughing.

shot.note: the whole treeline across the river moving at once

line.text: Titus. The woods.
Any standard! Get to any standard! Don't look for your own!
Tenth! Remember who you are. Keep your heads, and take the shock.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Nervii attacked from the woods while the camp was being fortified; no time for helmets or shield covers; men fell in at the nearest standard; Caesar's brief words to the Tenth (BG 2.19-21).

flow.objective: Drive the Atrebates into the river

lines.text: No time for helmets! Fight where you stand!
They're blown! They've run all the way here!
Titus! Left! On your left!
Go down! Go down!
Into the river with them! The Tenth has the bank!

flow.provenance: Documented: the Ninth and Tenth drove the breathless Atrebates down into the river and crossed after them (BG 2.23).
Documented: the Ninth and Tenth followed the Atrebates into the river, cut many down as they struggled across, crossed themselves and renewed the fight on disadvantageous ground (BG 2.23).

lines.text: They're in the river! After them! Don't stop in the water, it's deeper than it looks!

arrive.text: Up the bank! They're turning round! They're turning!

flow.objective: Break them on the far bank

lines.text: Up the bank! Don't let them form!
Keep your feet! The mud's worse than they are!
Titus! Out of the mud! Out!
Go down! Gods, go down!
Far bank's ours. Titus. Look back at the hill. Look at the camp.
lines.dir: the joy going out of it

flow.provenance: Documented: across the river, on disadvantageous ground, the Ninth and Tenth again routed the Atrebates who turned to oppose them (BG 2.23). New situation: a tight r6 bank, fighting uphill out of the river; three waves. Act I finisher: desperate.

flow.location: Far bank of the Sabis

shot.note: behind them, smoke over the Roman camp on the hill

line.text: Arrius! The camp's open behind us. Find the general on the right wing. Tell him the Ninth and Tenth hold the far bank.
Sir.
Titus, take someone with you.
Hold them here, Sextus.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL PLACEMENT. Justification for putting the centurion beside Caesar: he is sent as a runner from the Tenth on the left to Caesar on the right. Context documented: the camp front and left were exposed (BG 2.23); camp followers and Treveri cavalry fled (BG 2.24).

flow.objective: Run to Caesar on the right wing

lines.text: Fourth cohort's centurions are all dead. All of them. The standard's gone.

flow.provenance: Documented: Treveri cavalry fled reporting a Roman defeat (BG 2.24); all centurions of the Twelfth's fourth cohort killed and its standard lost (BG 2.25). The run itself is fictional. Traversal through a broken camp.

flow.location: Right wing, the Twelfth Legion's crush

shot.note: standards bunched together, men too crowded to swing; Caesar on foot, no shield

line.text: You. Your shield. Give it to me.
line.dir: to a man in the rear rank

line.text: Baculus! Sextius Baculus, sit down before you fall down. That's an order.
Standards forward! Open your ranks! Give yourselves room for the sword!
General! The Ninth and Tenth hold the far bank!
Then you're the only good news on this hill. Stand by me, Arrius.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar snatched a shield from a soldier in the rear, went to the front rank, called the centurions by name, ordered the standards forward and the ranks opened; P. Sextius Baculus was exhausted with wounds (BG 2.25). The words to Baculus are invented. Fictional: the centurion's arrival.

lines.text: Look at me, not at them! Push!
Good! Again!
He's in the front rank! The general's in the front rank!
Arrius! Stay on your feet!
For him! For him!

flow.provenance: First brute (unblockable overhead) of the game. The hold ends on a scripted knockdown that leads into ch03_s04.

flow.location: Right wing, the Twelfth Legion's crush

shot.note: from the ground: a Nervian axe coming down; Caesar steps over him and takes it on the borrowed shield
the borrowed shield, split

line.text: Up, Arrius. I'm not finished with you.

shot.note: the Tenth pouring down the far hill from the captured enemy camp

line.text: Tenth! Tenth!
Labienus. Of course it's Labienus.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: Caesar personally saving the centurion. Documented context: Labienus, from the captured enemy camp, sent the Tenth back to relieve the hard-pressed legions (BG 2.26).

lines.text: Miss us?
That's it. That's the Nervii.

flow.provenance: Documented: the arrival of the Tenth turned the battle (BG 2.26-27).

flow.location: The riverbank at sunset

shot.note: heaps of Nervian dead at the river; the last of them stood on the bodies to fight

line.text: Look at them. They stood on their own dead to reach us.
Remember them. Remember that men like that were beaten by you.

shot.note: Gavius bandaging the centurion's arm by the fire, gold light

line.text: He saved you? Himself? With his own shield?
Someone else's shield.
We will never hear the end of this.
Never. I'll tell it at your funeral.
I'll sing it.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Nervii fought from heaps of their own dead; Caesar praises their courage (BG 2.27). Caesar's words to the centurion and the campfire are fictional. End of Act I.

chapters.title: Fifty-Three Thousand
chapters.summary: A town that laughed at short Romans surrenders, breaks its surrender, and is sold entire. Fufius is asked to count.

flow.location: Siege works before the town of the Aduatuci, rain

shot.note: a siege tower under construction far from the wall; Gauls jeering from the battlements

line.text: They're asking how such little men mean to move a tower that size. With what hands.
Tell them with these hands. And tell them I'm tall, for a Roman.
I told them. They laughed harder.
I've been lent to the quaestor, centurion. He wants a man who can count.
Count what?
Whatever's left, he says.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Aduatuci mocked the Romans' small stature and the distant tower (BG 2.30). Fictional: Ritumara's translation, Fufius's secondment.

flow.objective: Raise the rampart round the town

lines.text: Twelve feet high, fifteen miles round, all for one town. That's a lot of rampart for a joke about our height.
They're asking if you dig because you're too short to climb.
lines.dir: translating from the wall, enjoying it

lines.text: Don't answer. Dig. Answering is what they want.
Gate's opening! Here they come again!

flow.provenance: Documented: the Aduatuci made frequent small sallies when the army arrived, until hemmed in by a rampart twelve feet high and fifteen miles round; vineae were brought up and a mound raised (BG 2.30). Fictional: the lines.

flow.objective: Drive the sally back to the gate

lines.text: Shields! Meet them before they reach the works!
Push them back to their gate! Back to their gate!
Titus, give ground! Back to the ditch!
Good. One less of them laughing.
Back through the gate. They'll stay inside now.

flow.provenance: Documented: frequent sallies and small skirmishes before the town was hemmed in (BG 2.30). Act II: two waves of three and four; finisher style practiced.

flow.objective: Move the tower up to the wall

lines.text: Small men coming! Very small men!
Together, on my word. Heave.
They've stopped laughing.

flow.provenance: Documented: the tower was moved up to the wall, startling the defenders (BG 2.31).

flow.location: Before Caesar's tribunal at the siege lines

shot.note: Aduatucan envoys kneeling in the mud; Ritumara beside them

line.text: He says the Romans must make war with the help of the gods, to move such machines so fast.
He asks one thing. Let them keep their weapons. Their neighbours hate them and would kill them unarmed.
I'll spare the town, from my custom, not their merit, if they surrender before the ram touches the wall.
The weapons they give up. I'll order the neighbours to leave them alone, and the neighbours will obey.

shot.note: weapons thrown from the wall into the ditch until the heap nearly reaches the top

line.text: Look at that pile. Nearly to the top of the wall. That's the war done.

flow.provenance: Documented: the envoys' speech, Caesar's reply and the heap of surrendered arms (BG 2.31-32). Lines condensed; the envoy's words are given through the interpreter (fictional device).

flow.objective: Walk the works in the third watch

lines.text: He had every man out of the town before dark. So nobody bothers the townspeople in the night. That's like him.
I'm telling Vibia these ones are the grandsons of the Cimbri. Her grandfather fought the Cimbri. Or ran from them.
I counted the arms pile, centurion. Four thousand swords on the top layer alone. Then I stopped.
Why?
Nobody asked me to count it. I just wanted to know.
Two to one they kept some back. Nobody gives up all their swords. I wouldn't.
Who's taking the bet?
Nobody. That's what worries me.
They asked me to tell you they are grateful for the general's terms.
Are they?
They asked me to tell you.
lines.dir: a beat; she lets him hear it

lines.text: Quiet up there. Too quiet for people who lost a war this afternoon.
They're tired.
Nobody's that tired.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar had the gates shut at evening and the soldiers withdrawn from the town lest the townspeople be harmed by night (BG 2.33); the Aduatuci were descended from the Cimbri and Teutones (BG 2.29); they had secretly kept back about a third of their arms (BG 2.32). Fictional: the watch and every exchange.

flow.location: The works, third watch

shot.note: night; the town wall a black line; below it, something moving across the ground, many shapes

line.text: Centurion. Below the wall. Lots of them.
Light the signal. As the general ordered.

shot.note: the signal fire catches on the rampart; along the line, fort after fort answers it

flow.provenance: Documented: the night sally in the third watch; the alarm was given at once by fires, as Caesar had ordered in advance, and men ran from the nearest fort (BG 2.33). Fictional: who lit it.

flow.objective: Hold the works in the third watch

lines.text: Fires on the hill! They kept their swords! To the rampart!
Bark shields! They've made shields out of bark!
Titus, back! Back onto the rampart!
Neat. Very neat, centurion.
I tried to count them. I stopped.

flow.provenance: Documented: the night sally with concealed arms and shields of bark and wicker; fire signals; about 4,000 killed (Caesar's figure, BG 2.33). Act II finisher: practiced.

flow.location: Inside the broken gates, morning

shot.note: the whole population of the town in the square, sorted into lots by traders with tablets; nobody is struck on camera

title.sub: persons reported sold, according to the buyers' count given to Caesar (BG 2.33)

line.text: Our tallies say fifty-three thousand, centurion. The quaestor will have the exact figure tonight.
I keep losing count. They won't stand still.
Then make them stand still.
line.dir: practical, not unkind; he doesn't hear himself

line.text: Yes, centurion.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar sold the whole town as booty; 53,000 persons reported by the buyers (BG 2.33). This is Caesar's reported figure, not a verified count. Fictional: the exchange.

flow.objective: Bring Fufius's tally to the quaestor

lines.text: My wife's father was sold once. Pirates. He bought himself back in eleven years.
Fifty-three thousand. If every one of them owned a chicken.
Bassus.
I'm only saying. That's a lot of chickens.
I asked one of them her name. She told me. I've forgotten it already.
The Aedui will buy some. We need hands for the harvest.
Your people buy slaves?
Everyone's people buy slaves, centurion. Better us than an Italian estate. We feed ours, and they know the language.

flow.provenance: Walk through the sale. Gallic elites also traded in slaves; Ritumara's view is hers, not the game's verdict.

flow.location: Caesar's tribunal at the siege lines, evening

shot.note: the tribunal in the rain; behind it, out of focus, the lots of people being led off down the road in files

line.text: The quaestor's figure, general. Fifty-three thousand, by the buyers' tallies. I checked them twice.
Thank you, Fufius. A clean count. I'll ask for you again.
Thank you, general.
line.dir: pleased, and then not sure why he is pleased

line.text: The Belgae are finished, Arrius. I'll write to the Senate tonight. They'll vote us a thanksgiving.
How many days, sir?
That depends on how well I write. And on how large the number is.
He makes it sound like a harvest.

title.sub: The thanksgiving Rome decreed on Caesar's letter, an honour granted to no one before (BG 2.35)

flow.provenance: Documented: the sale reported at 53,000 by the buyers (BG 2.33); on Caesar's letter a thanksgiving of fifteen days was decreed, an honour never before granted (BG 2.35). Plausible: Caesar writing that night. Fictional: the dialogue; Caesar praising Fufius begins Fufius's career as a tally clerk.

chapters.provenance: The Tenth is not named at the Aduatuci; Caesar's army was present in force. Presence: plausible.

chapters.title: The Bridge
chapters.place: Lower Meuse and the Rhine (locations debated)
chapters.summary: A camp of migrating families destroyed after their leaders are detained. Caesar explains, kindly and clearly, why it was necessary. Ten days later, a bridge across the Rhine.

flow.location: Roman camp near the Meuse, morning rain

title.sub: Between the Meuse and the Rhine, 55 BCE

line.text: New man from the levy, centurion. This is Decimus. Everyone calls him Tiro, because he is one.
I can carry anything, centurion. I carried my father's plough when the ox died.
Can you lose at dice?
I don't gamble.
You will.
Their chiefs walked into our camp this morning to apologise. Caesar's kept them. All of them.
Under truce, sir?
He says the truce died yesterday, with seventy-four of our horsemen. We march in an hour.

flow.provenance: Documented: German cavalry attacked during a truce, killing 74 of Caesar's cavalry; next day the German leaders came to the camp and Caesar detained them (BG 4.12-13). Labienus's presence and Tiro are not attested: plausible/fictional.

lines.text: Lesson one, Tiro. Never bet against the Tenth. Lesson two. Always bet against Fufius.
I still don't gamble.
Lesson three. Everyone says that once.
Gavius says the Germans only asked for land. Why not give them some?
The general says there's none spare in Gaul.
Could I ask him?
No.
Rain on the helmet, rain on the road, rain in the wine, and the Germans pay for all of it.
Second verse is ruder. Tiro's too young.
Eight miles in three lines and not a shout. They won't know we're here till we're in the carts.
Stay behind me today, boy. Right behind. Where I can feel you.

flow.provenance: Documented: the German envoys asked for lands, and Caesar replied there were none lying waste in Gaul to give (BG 4.7-8); the army marched eight miles in three lines and reached the German camp before it knew (BG 4.14). The Tenth is not named: presence plausible. Fictional: every exchange. Opimius's last cheerful song.

flow.location: Below the German wagon camp, rain

shot.note: the wagon ring ahead through rain; cooking smoke; nobody on watch

line.text: No sentries. Nobody giving orders. Their chiefs are in our camp, eating our bread.
Tenth. Quietly. Then all at once.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Germans were taken by surprise, leaderless, unable to decide whether to fight, defend the camp or flee (BG 4.14). Fictional: the lines.

lines.text: No leaders! They don't know what to do! Push!
Watch the wagons! They're under the wagons!
Tiro, behind me! Behind me, boy!
Did you see that, centurion? Did you see?
That's the fighters done. Titus. The rest are running.

flow.provenance: Documented: the leaderless German camp surprised; armed men resisted briefly among carts and baggage (BG 4.14). The Tenth is not named: presence plausible.

flow.location: The German wagon camp, after the fighting

shot.note: cavalry riding out past the wagons after fleeing women and children; seen from behind, at distance, no blows on screen

line.text: The cavalry's going after them. The families.

shot.note: a carved wooden horse, a child's, in the mud by a wheel

line.text: Where are they all going?
The river.

shot.note: hold; he says nothing

title.sub: Caesar's figure for the enemy's number. Roman dead: none. (BG 4.15, Caesar's claim)

flow.provenance: Documented: women and children fled and Caesar sent cavalry after them; the Germans, seeing their families killed, fled to the confluence of the Meuse and Rhine and many drowned; Caesar gives 430,000 as their number and no Roman dead (BG 4.14-15). Figures are Caesar's claims.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: killing of women and children by cavalry. Staged entirely off-screen: distance, sound, an object. No victims shown.

lines.text: Good pot, this. Somebody's grandmother's. She won't be wanting it.
lines.dir: cheerful; he means nothing by it

lines.text: Centurion. It's a shoe. It's very small.
Put it down, Tiro. Leave things in the mud. Always leave them in the mud.
I counted to a hundred and then I stopped watching the river.
Not a scratch on us. Not one man. I keep checking. I keep counting us.
The general wants me. Get them back to camp.

flow.provenance: Fictional walk through the documented aftermath: the families fled toward the confluence, the cavalry pursued, many drowned; Caesar reports no Roman dead (BG 4.14-15). DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: walk through the aftermath of the killing of families. No bodies on screen: abandoned carts, objects in the mud, the river at distance. Tiro's shoe is the only close object; it is held, not lingered on.

flow.location: Caesar's tent, night, rain on the leather

shot.note: lamp, maps, a bowl of olives; Caesar writing

line.text: Arrius. Come in out of that. You look like a drowned dog.
Your century?
All present, sir. Not a scratch.
Not one man lost, in the whole army. Write that down somewhere. You'll want to remember it.
Sir. Permission to speak.
You've had it since Vesontio.
Their chiefs were in our camp under truce. And the ones at the river were mostly women. Children.
Yes.
It was cruel. I won't insult you by calling it anything else.
Now count forward, not back.
Every tribe beyond the Rhine will know what happened here before the new moon. Next spring, none of them crosses.
No crossing, no war. No war, and I don't bury the Tenth in Gaul for ten years.
Be terrible once, and you won't have to be terrible again. That's the only mercy a general is ever offered.
Yes, sir.
Cato will want me handed over to the Germans for this. He'll make a beautiful speech.
Now. I want a bridge across the Rhine. Not boats. A bridge. Do you know why?
So they see it, sir.
So they see it. You're learning faster than my tribunes.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: the conversation and THE ARGUMENT (repeated in ch08_s03, ch11_s02, ch12_s03). Context documented: the detained leaders and the slaughter (BG 4.13-15), Caesar's reasons for crossing the Rhine so the Germans would fear for their own lands (BG 4.16), and his refusal to cross by boats as beneath Roman dignity (BG 4.17). Cato's proposal in the Senate to hand Caesar to the Germans comes from Plutarch (Caesar 22), not BG.

lines.text: Ten days, he says. A road across the Rhine in ten days.
Pull with your legs, Tiro, not your back. Your back belongs to the legion.
Sing, Opimius. You always sing for the piles.
Not today.

flow.provenance: Documented: paired piles driven aslant into the current with rammers; the work finished within ten days of collecting timber (BG 4.17-18). Rhythm-based labour; engineering as triumph.

flow.location: The Rhine bridge, the army crossing

shot.note: the bridge from above: a straight Roman line across a wild river; the column crossing

line.text: Ten days, Arrius. Tell your grandchildren it took ten days.
It's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen.
Yes.

shot.note: the far bank: empty fields, smoke from abandoned farms

line.text: The Sigambri have gone into the forests, sir. There's no one to fight.
There doesn't need to be. They saw it.

flow.provenance: Documented: the army led over; the Sigambri abandoned their lands for the woods (BG 4.18-19). Lines fictional.

flow.location: The bridgehead, eighteen days later

shot.note: the army coming back over the bridge; smoke on the German bank behind them, villages burning

title.sub: Villages burned and corn cut down; the Suebi waiting in their forests (BG 4.19)

line.text: The Suebi have gathered in the middle of their country, sir. They're waiting for us there.
Let them wait. They've seen us. The Sigambri have paid. The Ubii are safe. That's what we came for.
Arrius. Take the bridge down behind us.
Down, sir?
If we built it in ten days, they know we can build it again. That frightens them more than a bridge.

flow.provenance: Documented: after eighteen days beyond the Rhine, having burned the Sigambri's villages and cut their corn, Caesar judged he had done enough for honour and interest, returned to Gaul and cut down the bridge (BG 4.19). Caesar gives no reason for cutting it down; his line here is invention.

lines.text: Ten days up, two days down. Engineers. No wonder nobody likes them.
I carried that beam. That one there. I carried it in the rain.
Legs, Tiro. Not your back. It's the same beam going the other way.
There it goes. Like it was never there.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar cut down the bridge on his return (BG 4.19). The same task points and input rhythm as building it (ch05_g02), reversed.

flow.location: The Gallic bank of the Rhine, evening

shot.note: timbers of the bridge turning slowly in the current, going downstream; the far bank empty

line.text: It was the most beautiful thing I ever saw. Why build it at all?
So they saw it.
line.dir: Caesar's phrase; he does not notice

line.text: Who saw it?
Everyone.
Come on, Tiro. Supper. Legs, not back.

flow.provenance: Fictional. The first time the centurion repeats one of Caesar's phrases (ch05_s04 'They saw it'), three chapters before he repeats the argument (ch08_s03).

chapters.provenance: The Tenth is not named in BG 4.1-19. Presence: plausible.

chapters.title: The Eagle
chapters.summary: The eagle-bearer of the Tenth leaps into the sea. Gavius dies in the shallows. The centurion finishes his letter and leaves out the water.

flow.location: Aboard a transport off the British shore

shot.note: cliffs lined with armed Britons; chariots on the beach

line.text: If Caesar wanted me dead he could have done it on land.
To Vibia. We have crossed the Ocean. No one has ever done this. Bassus has been sick on a tribune.
line.dir: writing on his knee, reading aloud

line.text: What's past Britain?
More Bassus.

shot.note: the water over the side: deep, grey, the beach too far

line.text: It's too deep. We'll drown in our armour before we touch sand.
Jump, comrades, unless you want to hand the eagle to the enemy. I, at least, will do my duty to the Republic and my general.
The eagle's in the water!
Over the side, Tenth! Follow the eagle!

flow.provenance: Documented: the ships could not beach; the men hesitated at the depth; the eagle-bearer of the Tenth prayed, called out and leapt (BG 4.24-25). His words are paraphrased. Fictional: everything else.

lines.text: Stay by me, Tiro! Stay by me!
Can't find my feet! Can't hold the line!
Titus! Out of the deep water!
Good. Next.
Centurion! Gavius is down! Gavius!

flow.provenance: Documented: fighting in the water, unable to keep ranks, Britons attacking men as they came ashore (BG 4.24, 4.26). Skirmishers stand in for chariot-borne javelin men.

flow.location: The shallows

shot.note: lying in a hand's depth of water; calm

line.text: Finish the letter. You know how she likes it.
You'll finish it.
Don't tell her about the water. Titus. Finish it.
Centurion...
Leave him. Forward, Tiro. Forward!

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: Gavius's death, set in the documented surf fighting (BG 4.26).

lines.text: On me! Form on me!
Boats! The general's sending the boats!
Titus, your shield!
They're breaking. They're breaking!

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar sent boats with soldiers to wherever men were in trouble; the Romans reached the beach and routed the Britons (BG 4.26).

flow.objective: Find the century on the beach

lines.text: Seventy-eight of eighty, centurion. Licinius is on the second ship. And Gavius.
lines.dir: reading a wax tablet, wet through

lines.text: I wrote him down anyway. I didn't know what else to write.
Land. Solid land. I'm never getting on a boat again.
lines.dir: flat on his back in the sand

lines.text: We go home on one.
Then I'm staying. Tell my mother I'm a Briton now. Tell her the food is bad.
He had this in his belt. His stylus. He was going to teach me letters.
lines.dir: holding it out to the centurion

lines.text: Keep it. Learn them.
Cavalry ships never made it. The wind turned them back. So nobody's chasing anyone.
First time I've seen the general's luck run short. Don't tell him I said so.
I'll carry his kit. It's my turn. He always said it was my turn.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Britons were routed but could not be pursued because the cavalry transports had failed to reach the island (BG 4.26). Fictional: the roll call, Gavius's stylus passing to Tiro (found on Tiro's body in ch09_s03).

flow.objective: Bury Gavius, then beach the ships

lines.text: He said Gaul smelled better than Rome. He'd have hated this place.
Deeper. He hated the cold. Give him a decent depth.
That's deep enough, centurion. That's a good depth.
Now the ships. Full moon tonight, the sailors say. Big tides. Nobody told the sea we're here.

flow.provenance: Fictional burial; the same dig input as the camp ditch (ch03_g05) and every later work beat, and nobody makes a speech. Documented: the warships had been drawn up on the beach; that night the full moon brought the highest tides, unknown to the Romans (BG 4.29).

flow.location: The beach camp, night, storm

shot.note: Gavius's tablet and stylus in the centurion's hands

line.text: To Vibia, from her husband. We have crossed the Ocean. No one has ever done this.
line.dir: writing; reading back in Gavius's rhythm

line.text: The food is bad. The centurion is fair.
Your husband died bravely, at the head of his comrades.
He died in the water, being kind to a boy.
She doesn't need the water.
He told me to pull with my legs.
Storm's wrecked half the ships. We're stuck on an island at the end of the world. Lucky we brought the general.

flow.provenance: Fictional scene. Documented context: a storm wrecked and damaged many ships at the anchorage (BG 4.28-29).

flow.location: The camp gate on the British shore, days later

shot.note: the beached fleet being patched with timber from the wrecks; inland, a column of dust over the trees

title.sub: One legion foraging in the only field left unreaped (BG 4.32)

line.text: That's too much dust for men cutting corn.
The cohorts on the gate, with me. The rest arm and follow. Arrius, you're on the gate.
How does he see these things?
He looks.

flow.provenance: Documented: while the ships were repaired with timber and bronze from twelve wrecks (BG 4.31), the guards at the gate reported more dust than usual where a legion had gone to forage; Caesar took the cohorts on duty and ordered the rest to arm and follow (BG 4.32). Plausible: the Tenth's cohort on the gate.

lines.text: To them! Shields on the left! They throw and run!
Chariots! They throw, they jump down, they're back up again! Gods, they're quick!
Titus! Javelins from the left!
Neat. Gavius would have put that in a letter.
We'd put our shields down to reap! We were reaping!

flow.provenance: Documented: the Britons had hidden in the woods, fell on the legion as it reaped with arms laid aside, and surrounded it with cavalry and chariots; chariot fighters drove about throwing weapons, then leapt down to fight on foot; on Caesar's arrival they paused and he withdrew to camp (BG 4.32-34). New behaviour: javelin skirmishers first, warriors after, the field ends with the enemy withdrawing. Staged on the beach arena for lack of an inland field.

flow.location: Aboard a transport, the crossing back to Gaul, night

shot.note: the same deck as the crossing out; Gavius's place on the bench is empty and nobody sits in it

title.sub: Hostages doubled; the fleet sails before the equinox (BG 4.36)

line.text: Back on a boat. I'm a Briton now. Nobody asked me.

shot.note: Tiro scratching letters on a wax tablet with Gavius's stylus, very slowly

line.text: How do you write Vibia? Is it a V or a B?
Who are you writing to?
Gavius's wife. Someone should tell her he was kind to me. The centurion's letter didn't say.
It's a V. Write it big. She'll like that.

flow.provenance: Documented context: Caesar doubled the hostages and sailed back to the continent before the equinox (BG 4.36). Fictional: the scene. Tiro writes what the centurion's letter left out.

chapters.provenance: Documented: the Tenth's eagle-bearer at the landing (BG 4.25).

chapters.title: Race and Name
chapters.summary: Revenge for a lost legion. Burning becomes a day's work. Caesar remembers Gavius's name and his widow's pay.

flow.objective: Follow the road into the clearing

lines.text: Fourteen villages since the Mosa, centurion. I've stopped writing the names. Nobody's going to ask for them.
Is it always like this now? The smoke?
It's like this where we've been.
It's everywhere we've been.
lines.dir: not a complaint; working it out

lines.text: The Remi and the rest are in the woods ahead of us. Gaul plundering Gaul, by invitation.
Bassus has a book on which tribe brings back the most cattle.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar invited the neighbouring states to plunder the Eburones (BG 6.34); every village and building in sight was burned (BG 6.43). Cold open before the Act III title: a walk under smoke into the clearing. Fictional: the exchanges.

flow.location: Forest clearing in the land of the Eburones

title.sub: The forests of the Eburones, 53 BCE

shot.note: centurions around Caesar in a clearing; smoke already rising in the distance

line.text: He hasn't shaved since the news about Sabinus.
Neither have I. Nobody calls it grief.
A legion and five cohorts. Sabinus and Cotta, because Ambiorix asked them nicely to leave their camp.
I've invited every neighbour of the Eburones to come and plunder them. Let Gauls die in these woods, not my legionaries.
When we're finished, the name Eburones will need explaining.

flow.provenance: Documented: Sabinus and Cotta's legion and five cohorts destroyed after Ambiorix persuaded them to leave camp (BG 5.26-37); Caesar invited neighbouring states to plunder the Eburones so Gauls rather than legionaries would risk the woods, and so 'the race and name' might be annihilated (BG 6.34). Caesar letting his beard grow until avenged is from Suetonius (Divus Julius 67), not BG. The Tenth is not named here: plausible.

lines.text: Best-paid arson in the world, lads.
Forty-one head of cattle. Mark it. Forty-one.
There's no one here, centurion. Where are they all?
In the woods. Watching.

flow.provenance: Documented: every village and building the army could see was burned, cattle driven off (BG 6.43). The steadings are empty in this beat; the inhabitants have fled into the woods (BG 6.34). Burning as routine labour, same input rhythm as camp-building.

flow.objective: Clear the ambush in the forest

lines.text: In the bracken! Ambush!
Like you showed me, centurion!
Titus! Behind!
Clean.
Next steading.

flow.provenance: Documented: scattered Eburones laid ambushes for soldiers separated in the woods (BG 6.34). Act III finisher: surgical.

lines.text: Same as the last one, lads. Roof, corn, cattle. Home by dark.
lines.dir: cheerful, a work song in it

lines.text: There's bread on the table. It's still warm.
Burn the table.
Prisoner says Ambiorix was here an hour ago. Four horsemen with him. Still in sight, he says.
Then his friends are close. Watch the trees.

flow.provenance: Documented: all villages and buildings burned, corn consumed or flattened so that anyone hiding would starve; prisoners repeatedly said Ambiorix had just been seen fleeing with four horsemen (BG 6.43). The steading is empty; its people are in the woods. Same input rhythm as ch07_g01.

lines.text: Out of the smoke! They're in the yard!
They're fighting for the house! It's on fire and they're fighting for it!
Titus! The roof's coming down! Out of the doorway!
Clean.
Six head of cattle. Mark it. And those.
lines.dir: pointing his stylus at the yard

flow.provenance: Plausible: scattered Eburones attacked small parties among the woods and steadings (BG 6.34). New situation: a cramped r5 yard inside a burning steading; three waves of three, a brute in the middle wave. Act III finisher: surgical.

flow.location: A burning steading at dusk

shot.note: Caesar on foot among the burning buildings, his horse led behind

line.text: Arrius. Walk with me.
Your Gavius. The letter-writer, who died in the surf. Did his widow get his savings from the burial club?
You remember him, sir?
I remember every man who dies for me. It's the cheapest thing I do, and the most valuable. Don't tell anyone.
Make sure she's paid. Tell the quaestor I said so.
Your men are good at this.
They're good at everything, sir.
Yes. That's what frightens the Gauls.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: Caesar remembering the dead comrade's name (North Star 3). Context: the devastation of the Eburones (BG 6.43).

flow.location: Durocortorum of the Remi, morning

shot.note: a field outside the town filling with the chiefs of Gaul and their retinues; Roman cohorts at the edges

title.sub: Caesar summons a council of Gaul (BG 6.44)

line.text: Centurion. You've been in the Eburones' country. You smell of it.
Everyone does.
No. Only the ones who were there.

flow.provenance: Documented: after devastating the country Caesar led the army back to Durocortorum of the Remi and summoned a council of Gaul (BG 6.44). Fictional: the exchange.

flow.objective: Take your place at the council

lines.text: I've a list of every chief here, centurion. The ones who didn't come are forbidden fire and water.
I have to write down what that means. It means everything. I'm writing everything.
Centurion. What's the custom of our ancestors?
Don't ask him that, Tiro. Just stand where he puts you.
Book's closed on this one, centurion. Nobody would take the other side.

flow.provenance: Documented: the inquiry into the conspiracy of the Senones and Carnutes; those who fled the trial were forbidden fire and water (BG 6.44). Fictional: the exchanges. Leads straight into ch07_s03.

flow.location: Council of Gaul at Durocortorum of the Remi

shot.note: Gallic chiefs assembled in a square of Roman troops

line.text: Acco devised the conspiracy of the Senones and Carnutes. He is sentenced after the custom of our ancestors.

shot.note: the camera stays on the faces of the watching chiefs and on Ritumara; the punishment is behind the crowd
later; the square empty

line.text: He made every chief in Gaul stand and watch.
That was the point.
I know it was the point. I translated it.
My brother asked me tonight whose side the Aedui are on. I told him: whichever side is still standing.
That's wise.
No. It's tired.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar held a council of Gaul at Durocortorum and punished Acco 'after the custom of our ancestors' (BG 6.44); the phrase is generally read as flogging and beheading (interpretation, not stated in the text). Fictional: Ritumara's presence and the dialogue.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: judicial execution (flogging and beheading). Off-screen; sound only, camera on witnesses.

chapters.provenance: The Tenth is not named in the operations of BG 6.29-44. Presence: plausible.

chapters.title: Avaricum
chapters.summary: Hunger, a terrace, fire and rain. In the sack, Tiro questions an order, and the centurion answers him in Caesar's words.

flow.location: Siege lines before Avaricum, cold, hungry

shot.note: men at work on the siege terrace, thin; Caesar on foot going from legion to legion

line.text: If the hunger's too much, tell me, and I'll raise the siege. I mean it. No one will think less of you.
And go home and say we got peckish? Not the Tenth, sir.
We'll eat the wall if we have to.
I was afraid you'd say that.
What happened at Cenabum?
They killed the Roman traders there. All of them. I knew one. He sold ink.

flow.provenance: Documented: severe hunger; Caesar offered the legions, one by one, to raise the siege, and they begged him not to, wanting to avenge the Romans massacred at Cenabum (Genabum) (BG 7.3, 7.17). The Tenth is not named at Avaricum: presence plausible.

flow.objective: Go round the century before the watch

lines.text: You said no to raising the siege before he'd finished asking.
He knew the answer.
He always does. That's why he asks.
Third day of beef and no bread. I never thought I'd be sick of meat, centurion.
Complain to the general.
I can't. He offered to take us home. Now nobody's allowed to complain.
The grain officer they killed at Cenabum had my name, centurion. Fufius Cita. No relation. I keep writing it down.
Centurion. Look. I wrote it myself. Dear mother, I can write now.
lines.dir: holding up a wax tablet; Gavius's stylus

lines.text: Who taught you?
His stylus did. I just held it.

flow.provenance: Documented: for several days the soldiers had no corn and lived on cattle driven from distant villages, yet said nothing unworthy of Rome; Caesar offered to raise the siege and they begged him not to (BG 7.17); C. Fufius Cita, Caesar's grain officer, was among the Romans killed at Cenabum (BG 7.3; this translation prints Fusius). Fictional: the exchanges; the namesake is coincidence the character notices.

flow.objective: Bring the cattle in from the villages

lines.text: Thirty-one head from four villages. Mark it. Four villages we'll never see again.
Beef for breakfast. Beef for supper. Beef in my dreams, and the beef is winning.
Riders on the ridge! Their horse and their runners! They want the herd!

flow.provenance: Documented: cattle driven from remote villages kept the army alive (BG 7.17); Vercingetorix's cavalry and the light infantry who fought among them lay in wait for Roman foragers (BG 7.18). The same work rhythm as the terrace.

lines.text: Between them and the pen. Nobody touches the herd.
They're cutting the ropes! They're going for the calves!
Titus! On your right! Right!
Did you see that? I'll do it like that next time. Exactly like that.
Twenty-nine head. Two lost. Mark it.

flow.provenance: Plausible: an attack on the foragers' herd at the siege lines, of the kind Vercingetorix prepared (BG 7.18). Act III: two waves of four. Finisher style surgical.

lines.text: Eighty feet high, the engineers say. I'm not even five and a half.
Twenty-five days. Every basket counted.
I can carry two, centurion.
Carry one, and carry it fast.

flow.provenance: Documented: a terrace 330 feet broad and 80 feet high raised in 25 days despite cold and rain (BG 7.24).

lines.text: They're under the terrace! Fire in the timbers!
Another one's taken his place at the gate. Another one!
Then kill that one too.
Titus, step back! You're alone up there!
Like gutting a fish.
Terrace holds. Mark it.

flow.provenance: Documented: a night sortie fired the terrace from a mine beneath it; before a gate, Gauls throwing tallow and pitch were killed one after another and each replaced by the next (BG 7.24-25).

flow.location: Behind the vineae, heavy rain

line.text: They've left the walls for the rain. Go now, quietly. The first men on the wall will be rewarded.
Second century, with me. Ladders.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar used a rainstorm when the guards were slack, and promised rewards to those first on the wall (BG 7.27).

lines.text: Up! Up, up!
Centurion! They're running for the gates!
Into the streets. Keep together.
They're throwing their weapons down, Titus. All along the wall. They're throwing them down.
Cenabum! Remember Cenabum! Nobody's taking prisoners for the traders today!
lines.dir: a man of another legion, hoarse, running past

lines.text: Corn. I can smell corn. Granaries, lads, there's granaries.

flow.provenance: Documented: the defenders threw down their arms and fled to the far side of the town; the soldiers, enraged by the massacre at Cenabum and the toil of the siege, spared neither the old, nor women, nor children (BG 7.28). DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED.

lines.text: Second century. Keep together. Down the street to the market.

flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: the walk into a town being sacked. Nothing is shown: closed doors, running men with their backs to camera, sound from side streets. No victim is on screen.

flow.location: A street inside Avaricum

shot.note: a closed house door; Tiro's hand on the doorpost

line.text: Centurion. There are women in there. Old men. They don't have weapons.
I know.
The order was the wall, sir. We have the wall.
It's cruel. I won't insult you by calling it anything else.
line.dir: calm, almost gentle; Caesar's cadence exactly

line.text: Now count forward, not back.
Every town in Gaul will hear about Avaricum before the new moon. Next spring, they open their gates.
Open gates, no sieges. No sieges, and I don't bury you in Gaul.
Be terrible once, and you won't have to be terrible again.
Yes, centurion.

shot.note: long hold on the centurion; the door stays shut; nothing is seen

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL scene inside the documented sack: Caesar writes that the soldiers spared neither the old, nor women, nor children (BG 7.28). The centurion repeats Caesar's ch05 argument almost word for word (North Star 3).
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: implied killing of unarmed civilians by the player's men on the player's order. Nothing is shown; the door closes and sound drops out.

flow.location: The market square of Avaricum, next morning

shot.note: soldiers eating; Tiro apart, not eating; Opimius cleaning the standard's pole

line.text: Corn! Whole granaries of it. We eat tonight, lads.
No captives to count. That's a first.
You said that very well. To the boy.
It's true.
I know it's true. That isn't what I said.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar gives about 40,000 inside and fewer than 800 escaping; he says no one was intent on plunder (BG 7.28). These are Caesar's claims. Fictional: the scene.

chapters.provenance: The Tenth is not named at Avaricum; most of Caesar's legions were there (BG 7.10-11). Presence: plausible.

chapters.title: Gergovia
chapters.summary: Caesar halts the Tenth; the rest of the army runs at the wall. The women on the wall shout Avaricum. Tiro, carrying the centurion's message, does not come back.

flow.location: Roman lesser camp below Gergovia, dawn

shot.note: muleteers in helmets riding around the hills pretending to be cavalry

line.text: They've put helmets on the muleteers. Helmets! On Corvus! He's riding round the hill pretending to be cavalry.
The Gauls will see Corvus and surrender out of pity.
We take their camps on the slope, and we stop. Whatever happens, when the trumpet sounds, we stop.
Let me carry the messages today, centurion. I'm the fastest in the century.
To the legate of the Eighth, when the trumpet goes. Tell him the Tenth has halted. Then straight back to me.
Straight back.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar's ruse of muleteers in helmets posing as cavalry (BG 7.45); his intention to take the camps on the slope and not to assault the town (BG 7.45-47, 7.52). The Tenth was with Caesar (BG 7.47). Fictional: Tiro as runner (deliberate mirror of ch03_s02).

flow.objective: Form up below the Gallic camps

lines.text: I put Gavius's stylus in my belt, centurion. For luck. He won't mind.
Run fast. Come straight back.
Book on Corvus, lads. Two to one he falls off before the Gauls notice he's a muleteer.
Caesar told every legate twice. Take the camps, then stop. You heard him say stop?
I heard him.
Make sure the boy heard him.

flow.provenance: Documented: at dawn muleteers in helmets rode round the hills to look like cavalry; Caesar moved men in small parties to the lesser camp with standards covered and warned the legates to restrain their men from going too far (BG 7.45). Fictional: the exchanges.

flow.location: Below the Gallic camps on the slope, morning

shot.note: the slope up to Gergovia; the Gallic camps half empty, their men gone to the far hill after the muleteers

line.text: There's the signal.
Tenth. Up the slope. Take the camps. Then stop.

shot.note: Tiro already running toward the Eighth

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar gave the signal; the soldiers reached the wall of the camps quickly and took three of them (BG 7.45-46). Fictional: the lines; Tiro running for the Eighth (ch09_s01).

flow.objective: Take the camps on the slope

lines.text: Over the camp wall! Up the slope!
You didn't even break stride.
Halt here. Wait for the trumpet.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Romans took three Gallic camps on the slope so quickly that a king of the Nitiobriges escaped half-dressed (BG 7.46).

flow.location: Halfway up the slope of Gergovia

line.text: That's the recall. Tenth, halt! Halt!

shot.note: across a valley, the other legions still running uphill toward the town wall; a small figure among them

line.text: The others didn't hear it. They're going for the wall.

shot.note: women on the wall leaning out with outstretched hands, throwing down clothes and silver

line.text: They're shouting Avaricum. It's the only word I understand.
Where's Tiro?
He went with the message. He's with the Eighth. He's on the hill.

flow.provenance: Documented: the recall sounded; the Tenth, with Caesar, halted; the other legions, across a valley, did not hear and pressed to the wall; matrons on the wall begged the Romans not to kill women and children 'as they had done at Avaricum' (BG 7.47). The women's voices are not subtitled except the one word.

lines.text: Hold here. Nobody goes up that hill. Let them come to us.
Here they come! The whole hill!
Titus! You're out of the line!
They're pulling back. The Thirteenth's on the hill. They're pulling back.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Tenth, in reserve on more level ground, checked the Gallic pursuit, supported by cohorts of the Thirteenth (BG 7.51). Heaviest fight of the game so far.

lines.text: Petronius. Our centurion. He said he'd led us into it for glory. Told us to save ourselves. Then he went back to the gate.
lines.dir: a man of the Eighth, sitting up, holding his arm

lines.text: Corvus came back, centurion. The mules are fine. All the mules are fine.
I'm writing down the centurions as they carry them past. I've got nineteen. They say there's more.
The Eighth have come down. He's not with them, Titus. He's not with the Eighth.

flow.provenance: Documented: the legions that did not hear the recall pressed to the wall; L. Fabius and the men with him were killed and thrown down; M. Petronius of the Eighth held the gate so his men could escape (BG 7.47, 7.50; this translation prints Petreius); heavy losses (BG 7.51). The walk passes the Roman dead; no gore. Fictional: the exchanges.

flow.location: Foot of the slope, evening

shot.note: Tiro's body at the foot of the slope, almost back to the Tenth's line; the centurion kneeling
Gavius's stylus tucked in Tiro's belt

line.text: He was carrying your message.
He didn't wait for the signal.
Titus. He was carrying your message.
Then he should have carried it.

shot.note: the centurion takes the stylus

title.text: Forty-six centurions. Nearly seven hundred men.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: Tiro's death. Documented: the loss of 46 centurions and nearly 700 soldiers (Caesar's figures, BG 7.51).

flow.location: Assembly of the army, next day

shot.note: the whole army in ranks; Caesar alone in front

line.text: I admire your courage. Neither the camp walls, nor the mountain, nor the town wall could stop you.
And in the same measure I condemn your recklessness. You decided you knew more about victory than your general.
I want restraint and self-command from my soldiers. No less than courage.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar's address the day after, praising courage and censuring rashness (BG 7.52-53). Paraphrased and condensed.

flow.objective: Offer battle on the level ground

lines.text: In line. Let them see us. Let them see nobody's running.
That's for the Eighth! And that! Put that on the tablet, Fufius!
Titus! You're out of the line again!
The boy wanted to learn that one.
They won't come down to the flat. Not today. Mark it.

flow.provenance: Documented: after the assembly Caesar drew the army up in battle order on suitable ground; Vercingetorix would not come down to the level ground; a small, successful cavalry action followed (BG 7.53). Plausible staging: Gallic light troops probing the line; the infantry fighting is invention.

flow.objective: Walk back through the camp to the horse lines

lines.text: Forty-six centurions. I've written all of them now. In order of rank. The way he likes it.
I gave Tiro a pair of dice at the Meuse. He never threw them once. Not once. He didn't gamble.
lines.dir: turning the dice over in his hand

lines.text: The Aedui are packing. Her people. Caesar's letting them go.
I know.

flow.provenance: Documented: forty-six centurions lost (BG 7.51); Caesar let the Aeduan leaders go (BG 7.54). Fictional: the exchanges.

flow.location: The horse lines, Aeduan riders leaving

line.text: Caesar has given the Aeduan lords leave to go home. He knows why we're going. He lets us go anyway.
He won't have it said that he insulted you.
My brother is at Bibracte. My son is with him.
The women on the wall were shouting Avaricum. Were you there?
Yes.
Goodbye, Titus.
line.dir: the first time she has used his name

flow.provenance: Documented context: Caesar let the Aeduan leaders Eporedorix and Viridomarus go, despite seeing their treachery, so as not to seem to insult them or fear them; the Aedui then joined the revolt (BG 7.54-55). Fictional: Ritumara and her family.

chapters.provenance: Documented: the Tenth with Caesar at the recall (BG 7.47) and in reserve checking the pursuit (BG 7.51).

chapters.title: Alesia
chapters.summary: Perfect geometry from above. From the rampart, families who may not be fed. The red cloak turns the battle. Every soldier gets a human being as his share.

flow.location: The Roman lines at Alesia, from the heights

shot.note: the double ring of works around the hill town: ditches, rampart, towers, perfectly regular; magnificent

line.text: Eleven miles of works facing in. Fourteen facing out. Look at it, Arrius. Nobody has ever built anything like this.
He has eighty thousand men in there and grain for thirty days. I have shovels.
The men are calling the pits lilies.
Soldiers become poets when they're tired enough.

flow.provenance: Documented: the inner circuit of eleven miles and outer circuit of fourteen; Vercingetorix's 80,000 men and corn for about thirty days (as Caesar reports him saying); the soldiers' names for the obstacles (BG 7.69, 7.71, 7.73, 7.74). Labienus at Alesia: documented (BG 7.86). The Tenth is not singled out at Alesia: presence plausible.

lines.text: Eight rows. Three feet apart. Keep the lines straight.
Lilies. Very pretty. Tombstones with flowers on.
Opimius. Opimius. You've been on that stake an hour.
Straight. Good.

flow.provenance: Documented: cippi, lilies (eight rows of pits with fire-hardened stakes, three feet apart) and spurs (BG 7.73). Same input rhythm as the Rhine piles.

flow.location: The inner rampart

shot.note: from the rampart: the Mandubii, families with children, coming down between the lines toward the Roman works

line.text: No one comes over the rampart. Not one.
If we feed them, we feed Vercingetorix. He sent them out so that we would have to.
No one comes over. Not one.
line.dir: to his men, before Caesar has finished turning away

flow.provenance: Documented: the Mandubii were expelled with wives and children, begged to be received as slaves and fed, and Caesar posted guards on the rampart and forbade them to be admitted (BG 7.78). Caesar gives no reason in BG; his line here is invention. BG does not state their fate; Cassius Dio (40.40) says they perished between the lines.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: civilians, including children, refused food and left between the lines. Show at distance; no close-ups of suffering.

lines.text: They'll go back in. Bound to. Nobody's that stubborn.
Day two.
That woman's been holding the child up for an hour. So we can see it.
Don't look, then.
Day four.

rules.note: Stand the watch. Nothing to fight. The light changes between barks to mark days passing.

flow.provenance: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED. Fictional framing of the documented refusal (BG 7.78). The player's only task is to keep standing there.

flow.location: The upper camp, days later

shot.note: dawn; the outer hills black with men and horses, a mile off; behind the camp, the town walls crowded with people watching them arrive

title.sub: Caesar's figures: 8,000 horse and about 240,000 foot (BG 7.76)

line.text: That's all of Gaul. The whole of it came.
Commius is with them. The one who came to Britain for Caesar.
Two hundred and forty thousand, they're saying. I'll take their word for it.
Then they've come to the right place. We built the walls facing both ways.

flow.provenance: Documented: the Gallic relief army of 8,000 cavalry and about 240,000 infantry (Caesar's figures) under Commius and others, who had served Caesar in Britain, encamped on the hills a mile from the outer works (BG 7.76, 7.79). Fictional: the lines. Covers the time and place jump from the inner rampart (ch10_g02) to the upper camp (ch10_g03).

lines.text: They're over the ditch! Inside and outside at once!
Gaul in front, Gaul behind! Bloody Gaul everywhere!
Titus, we can't hold this!
Like gutting fish. A whole market of fish.
Six cohorts, on Caesar's order! Hold, Tenth. The general is coming himself.

flow.provenance: Documented: the relief army's attack on the weak upper camp while the besieged attacked from inside (BG 7.83-86). Presence of the Tenth here is plausible.

flow.location: The upper camp

shot.note: down the slope, a single scarlet cloak among grey cohorts: the most saturated colour since Act I

line.text: The cloak! It's him! He's come himself!
Tenth! Leave the javelins! Swords!
The cavalry's behind them. Push now and it's finished!

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar's arrival recognised by the colour of his cloak; the shout along the lines; the troops laid aside javelins for swords; cavalry appeared in the Gauls' rear (BG 7.88).

lines.text: You're not even looking at them.
It's over.
Now. All of it, now.
They're running into our horse! The horse is behind them!

flow.location: Before the Roman camp, the surrender

shot.note: Caesar seated at the head of the lines; the Gallic chiefs brought before him
he lays down his arms; no words

line.text: Six years, Arrius. Remember this day.
line.dir: very quietly, not turning his head

shot.note: the same overhead as ch10_s01; the geometry complete

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar seated at the fortifications before the camp; the chiefs brought; Vercingetorix surrendered and arms laid down (BG 7.89; this translation runs 7.88-89 together). The manner of his surrender (riding round, sitting at Caesar's feet) is from Plutarch (Caesar 27) and is not used here.

flow.location: The distribution of captives, below the camp

shot.note: a table with tablets; captives led up one by one and handed to soldiers; on the far side, the Aedui and Arverni held apart

line.text: Tenth Legion, second cohort, sixth century. One each. Your name on the tablet, or your mark.
Mine's got all his teeth. Look at that.
I'll take him off your hands, centurion. Good price for a fighting man.

shot.note: the captive is a man about his own age; the centurion does not look at him

line.text: Fufius. Do the paperwork.
