shot.note: Opimius sitting beside his captive, an old woman; neither speaks

line.text: Caesar is keeping the Aedui aside. We're useful again.
You're alive.
Because we're useful. Not because he's kind. You know the difference.
In the end it comes to the same thing.
Tascos asked if you were the soldier who would show him the eagle. I told him you were somebody else.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar kept back the Aedui and Arverni to win back their states and gave one captive to every soldier in the army as booty; about 20,000 were later restored to the Aedui and Arverni (BG 7.89-90). Fictional: Ritumara's capture with the relief army, all dialogue.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: enslavement of captives as individual plunder, including the player character's own captive. No violence shown.

chapters.provenance: Caesar's whole army was at Alesia; the Tenth is not singled out. Presence: plausible.

chapters.title: Winter
chapters.place: Winter quarters (unrecorded); the Eburones again; the Carnutes
chapters.summary: The same fire, the same jokes, fewer people. The centurion writes a recruit's letter in Gavius's words and answers his question in Caesar's. Sextus hears.

lines.text: Word from Bibracte, centurion. The winter legions get two hundred each. Centurions two thousand. Instead of plunder.
Instead of plunder! What's a war for? Tell the general I'll take the plunder, thank you.
Home.
It's a camp.
That's what I said.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar paid the soldiers of his winter campaign two hundred sesterces each and the centurions two thousand, instead of plunder (BG 8.4). Where the Tenth wintered is not recorded (BG 7.90). Cold open before the Act IV title: the march back through the south gate of the ch1 camp, now in snow.

flow.location: Tenth Legion lines, winter quarters, dusk

shot.note: the same framing as ch01_s01; same fire, same places; snow and ash on the ground; the centurion sits where Gavius sat

line.text: Book's open, lads. How long before the Bellovaci give in. I've got Opimius down for never.

shot.note: Opimius does not react

line.text: Your share from Alesia has cleared, centurion. Four hundred sesterces after the trader's cut.
Put it with the rest.
Centurion? They said you write letters for the men. I can't, you see.

shot.note: Gavius's stylus, the one taken from Tiro

line.text: Dear mother. The food is bad. The centurion is fair.
line.dir: already writing; no thought in it

line.text: That's Gavius's line. Gods, you even write like him.

shot.note: Sextus watching; no line

flow.provenance: Fictional. Mirrors ch01_s01 in blocking and framing (same camp layout reused, dressed for winter). Where the Tenth wintered in 52-51 is not recorded (BG 7.90 lists other legions' quarters).

lines.text: Is it always this cold, centurion?
Only in winter, Marcus. Rest of the year it's hot, and they're trying to kill you.
Firewood, nine loads. Thatch, two huts. Mark it.
lines.dir: the same voice he uses for cattle

flow.provenance: Fictional camp work; Hirtius describes soldiers' tents roofed with thatch in the winter of 52-51 (BG 8.5, at Cenabum). Same rhythm as every work beat. The recruit stands where Tiro stood.

lines.text: Tonight's word is Venus. Same as the night at Vesontio. I keep the old lists.
Centurion.
Quiet night.

flow.provenance: Mirror of ch01_g01: same people at the same positions; the goal is the same spot as the old praetorium fire, now an empty square.

lines.text: Shields up. Both of you. Come at me together.
Ooh. He'll feel that tomorrow. And the day after.
Careful, centurion.
Six down. Mark it.
lines.dir: he doesn't hear what he's said

flow.provenance: Fictional practice drill with wooden swords; the new men yield. Act IV finisher: unseeing; no finisher bark on purpose. Marcus waits in Gavius's old spectator spot for his own bout (ch11_g02).

lines.text: Wooden swords, centurion. You'll go easy?
Ah!
Titus. Titus, he's down. He's a boy.
Pay up, Opimius.

flow.provenance: Mirror of ch01_g02. Finisher style unseeing: the centurion puts the recruit down with a practice sword without looking at him. Opimius does not answer the bark this time.

flow.location: Beside the drill ground, after dark

shot.note: the recruit holding a cloth to his mouth

line.text: Centurion. They say in spring we go back into the Eburones' country. Bassus says you burned it already.
We did.
Then who's left to burn?
It's cruel. I won't insult you by calling it anything else.
Now count forward, not back. Every valley that hears of it stays home next spring.

shot.note: Sextus at the edge of the firelight

line.text: Those are his words.
They're true words.
You stop where he stops. You even breathe where he breathes.
Sextus.
You didn't look at that boy when you put him down. You didn't look.
He'll learn.
Yes. He will.

shot.note: as the centurion steps toward him, Sextus's hand has gone to his sword hilt; he did not decide to do it

line.text: Goodnight, centurion.

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION: the friend overhears and names the words. Context documented: in 51 Caesar again laid waste the country of Ambiorix (Eburones) 'by sword, fire and rapine' (BG 8.24-25, Hirtius); the Tenth's participation is not recorded.

flow.location: The country of Ambiorix, spring 51

shot.note: a glade of stumps and grey regrowth; one roundhouse standing in it, its thatch new

line.text: The order, centurion. Waste it of people, cattle and buildings. So that if he survives, his own will hate him for it.
Is this the valley? The one you burned?
Same valley. Grows back quicker than you'd think. Somebody's put a new roof on.
Fire the barn.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar marched to devastate the country of Ambiorix, wasting it of inhabitants, cattle and buildings so that any survivors would hate him and keep him out (BG 8.24), by sword, fire and rapine (BG 8.25). The Tenth's part is not recorded: plausible. Covers the jump from the winter camp to the valley.

lines.text: Back again! Same valley. I remember that barn.
Nine head of cattle. Mark it. Nine.

flow.provenance: Reuses the ch07 set, two years on: stumps, ash, regrowth, fewer buildings. Same task prompt rhythm as ch07_g01. Short.

lines.text: Centurion. It's Roman. A belt plate. Whose would it be?
lines.dir: holding up something green with age

lines.text: Sabinus's men, maybe. Three years ago.
Should I keep it?
Leave things where they are.
The first time, forty-one head of cattle. Today, nine. I've both tallies.
Next time I won't need a tablet.
Opimius won't bet any more, centurion. He won't do anything but sharpen. I've a book on when he'll speak.
Barn's done, centurion. Orders?
The next valley.
Yes, centurion.

flow.provenance: Plausible: the legion and five cohorts of Sabinus and Cotta were destroyed in the country of the Eburones three years earlier (BG 5.37, 6.32); the second devastation (BG 8.25). Fictional: the exchanges. Sextus now only calls him centurion.

lines.text: Like this, centurion? Low on the trunk?
Low on the trunk. Then the next one.
There. Nothing left to come back to. Lunch?

flow.provenance: Plausible detail of the documented devastation (BG 8.24-25): the order was to leave the country unable to support its people. The recruit learns the rhythm in one try.

flow.location: Roman camp in the land of the Carnutes, summer 51

shot.note: soldiers packed round the tribunal, shouting; a bound prisoner held behind the line of shields, not clearly seen

line.text: Give him to us! Gutruatus! Give him to us!

shot.note: Caesar lets the noise go on; then raises a hand; silence

line.text: Very well. The army has spoken.
Let it be written down that I did not want this.
Written down, general.

shot.note: later; Caesar mounting

line.text: Arrius. I'm riding south with the cavalry. Calenus will bring the legions after me.
Caninius has a town that thinks it can outlast me. One more summer, and they all know it.
I want you with me.
Sir.

flow.provenance: Documented (Hirtius): the Carnutes' leader Gutruatus (spelled Guturvatus in this translation; manuscripts vary) was given up; Caesar was 'forced' by the soldiers' clamour, 'contrary to his natural humanity', to have him whipped to death and beheaded (BG 8.38). Caesar then left Q. Calenus with two legions and hurried with all the cavalry to Caninius at Uxellodunum, knowing the Gauls understood his command had one summer left (BG 8.39). FICTIONAL PLACEMENT: Caesar asking for the centurion by name, which is the narrative justification for ch12.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: execution of a prisoner (flogged to death and beheaded) at the soldiers' demand. Off-screen; sound only.

chapters.provenance: Hirtius (Book VIII) does not record where the Tenth was in 51 BCE.

chapters.title: Uxellodunum
chapters.place: Uxellodunum (usually identified with the Puy d'Issolud)
chapters.summary: Caesar takes the town by killing its spring. In the command tent, the same warmth as Vesontio, the same praise, and the order about the hands. The centurion knows the words before Caesar says them. Then the work, and then supper.

flow.location: The valley below Uxellodunum

shot.note: a steep crag almost ringed by a river; Roman lines already closed round it; pale, flat daylight

line.text: Everyone is looking at the river. Look at the spring instead.

shot.note: a spring gushing out just under the town wall, on the one side the river doesn't cover

line.text: Three hundred feet of open ground, right under their walls. Take that, and they die of thirst.
We'll be digging under their slingers.
Yes. I thought you'd enjoy that.

flow.provenance: Documented (Hirtius): Caesar cut the defenders off from the river with archers, slingers and engines, then saw, alone, that the spring under the walls could be taken (BG 8.40-41). FICTIONAL PLACEMENT: the centurion rode south with Caesar's cavalry (see ch11_s03); Legio X is not attested at Uxellodunum.

lines.text: They're coming down for water. Jars on their backs and swords in their hands.
Thirsty lot this morning!
Centurion. Your left.
Nobody reached the water. Mark it.

flow.provenance: Documented: Caesar posted archers, slingers and engines against the easiest descents to stop the townsmen getting water, until they all had to fetch it from one place, the spring under the wall (BG 8.40-41). Plausible: an armed water party driven back at the works. Act IV: five per wave, no finisher barks; the men they kill are carrying jars.

flow.objective: Drive the mine toward the spring

lines.text: Digging! Finally, something I'm good at.
Sixty-foot mound. Ten-storey tower. They'll want the plans in Rome.
Gallery's under the spring. Mark it.

flow.provenance: Documented: vineae, a mound sixty feet high with a ten-storey tower, and mines driven toward the spring under constant skirmishing (BG 8.41).

flow.objective: Hold the works against the fire

lines.text: Barrels! Burning barrels coming down the slope!
Tallow and pitch! Smells like a festival!
Cohorts! Up the hill on every side, and shout as if you mean to take the wall!
Fires out. Works intact.

flow.provenance: Documented: burning barrels of tallow, pitch and wood rolled onto the works with a furious sally; Caesar ordered cohorts to climb on all sides and shout as a feint (BG 8.42-43). Finisher style unseeing; no finisher barks on purpose.

flow.location: Below the town gate

shot.note: the gate opens; thin, filthy men come out and lay down weapons; no one cheers

line.text: They say the gods killed the spring. They say no man could have done it.
Tell them it was engineers.
My son is a hostage at Bibracte. So I translate.

flow.provenance: Documented: the mines cut the veins of the spring; the defenders thought it the will of the gods, not the work of men, and surrendered (BG 8.43). Fictional: Ritumara's presence; Caesar demanded many hostages from Gallic states (e.g. BG 7.90), her son's status is invented.

lines.text: Book's open, centurion. Will he be consul again? Even money. Put a denarius on it, for old times.
Stand straight in front of him.
He notices everything.
He asked me this morning how many men bore arms in the town. I gave him the number. He didn't ask for names.

flow.provenance: Fictional. Mirror of ch01_g01: three men at the ch1 talker positions on the walk to the general; Sextus speaks Gavius's ch01 line from Gavius's place. Fufius already has the number Caesar will use (BG 8.44 gives none).

flow.location: Caesar's command tent below Uxellodunum, evening

shot.note: Command tent; same layout as ch01 praetorium: Caesar on the same kind of folding stool, table and jug at his elbow, lamp where the fire was [mirror of ch01_s02 shot 1]

line.text: Arrius. Come into the light. Let me look at you.
line.dir: warm, amused; does not get up

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: General.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: Second day of the mine. A beam came down at your end of the gallery.
You held it on your back until they shored it, and you never mentioned it. Calenus saw. You didn't see him.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: It seemed simpler, sir.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: It always seems simpler, to the men who can do it.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: I'm told Bassus is running a book on whether I'll be consul again.
I can have him flogged.
Don't you dare. What are the odds?
Even, sir.
Put me down for a denarius. He still owes me one from Vesontio.

shot.note: Caesar pours wine into a plain cup and holds it out [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: Drink. It's terrible. Labienus isn't here to buy it.

shot.note: tighter; Caesar serious [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: Eight summers. There isn't a valley in Gaul that doesn't know what the Tenth can do.
One last piece of business, and Gaul is quiet.
The men who bore arms in that town. I want their hands.
line.dir: the same voice; nothing changes in it

line.text: Not their lives. Their hands. Let them walk home, and let every valley see them.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]
Caesar sees the hesitation; his face softens [extension beyond ch01_s02]

line.text: Titus.
line.dir: the first time he has used the name; tender

line.text: Everyone in Gaul knows I'm not a cruel man. That's why this will work.
It's cruel. I won't insult you by calling it anything else.

shot.note: the centurion's lips begin to move with Caesar's words, silently; his face otherwise still

anim.note: silent mouthing in sync with Caesar's next lines; no voice

line.text: Count forward, not back.
line.dir: on the centurion's extreme close-up; Caesar's voice slightly off-axis

line.text: Every town that thinks it can wait me out will see these men on the roads. No one else rebels. No one else dies.
Be terrible once, and you won't have to be terrible again.
line.dir: on the centurion's extreme close-up; the centurion's lips arrive at 'again' a fraction before Caesar's voice

shot.note: tighter; Caesar serious [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: Go on. And Titus. I'm glad you're with me. I always have been.

shot.note: [mirror of ch01_s02]

line.text: Yes, sir.

shot.note: same frame as shot 1 [mirror of ch01_s02]

flow.provenance: FICTIONAL INVENTION; mirrors ch01_s02 shot for shot (same nine shots, same lenses, same blocking at the same coordinates) before extending. Documented basis (Hirtius): Caesar, confident his leniency was known to all and that he would not be thought cruel by nature, and seeing no end to revolts if others imitated this one, cut off the hands of all who had borne arms and spared their lives so the punishment would be conspicuous (BG 8.44). Number of victims is not given.
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: content of the mutilation order (spoken, not shown). Also review Caesar's tenderness and the use of 'Titus'.

flow.location: The open ground before the town gate

shot.note: the prisoners seated in rows on the grass, guarded; the camera stays behind the centurion

line.text: Those who bore arms against Rome will lose their hands. Their lives are spared. They will go home.
line.dir: reading from a tablet; clear, unhurried

shot.note: she goes on speaking after the sentence is translated: more words, untranslated, to the prisoners only

line.text: What did you tell them?
What you said.
And the rest?
That was for them.

shot.note: she walks down to the road and does not look back

flow.provenance: Fictional staging of the documented sentence (BG 8.44).
flow.approvalNote: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: announcement of the sentence to the victims. Nothing is carried out on screen. Ritumara's Gaulish is a sound cue, never subtitled, never written; do not invent Gaulish text.

lines.text: Two hundred and twelve. Mark it. Next.
Come on, lads. Done by supper and there's pork.
Same as the stakes at Alesia. Find the rhythm and it goes quick.

flow.provenance: DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUIRED: the player enables the mutilation. STAGING: the work happens behind a screen of mantlets and men's backs, below frame. The player walks between three ordinary prompts. The sound bed is the same work rhythm as camp-building and stake-driving, with no screams. Camera stays at chest height on faces. No finisher, no combat input. The tally number is invented; Hirtius gives none.

flow.location: The camp below Uxellodunum, late afternoon

shot.note: pale daylight, washed-out; men eating, mending, washing; the ordinary end of a working day

line.text: Supper, centurion. Pork. Real pork.
All in order, centurion. Nothing outstanding.

shot.note: Opimius scouring his blade with sand, methodically
the centurion sits down beside Sextus

line.text: Centurion.

shot.note: he looks down at his hands; they are clean; hold
the camp goes on around him; no one looks at him

flow.provenance: Fictional. No music, no hero shot, no speech. Hell become ordinary (North Star 4). Hold long; no cut to credits.

chapters.provenance: Book VIII is by Aulus Hirtius. Legio X is NOT attested at Uxellodunum; Caesar came with the cavalry, Calenus followed with two unnamed legions (BG 8.39). The centurion's presence is a fictional placement justified in ch11_s03.
